client: I just got my exam grade back and it was way lower than I expected. I feel like I'm failing at everything because I can't keep up this perfect GPA anymore, and the pressure is making me so anxious. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help since the grade is already set in stone.
therapist: It sounds like this grade has left you feeling overwhelmed and questioning your abilities, especially with the pressure to maintain that perfect GPA. While the grade itself can't be changed, exploring how you're interpreting this situation might help ease some of that anxiety. What thoughts come up when you think about not meeting your own expectations?

client:
I just keep thinking that if I can't get perfect grades, then I'm not good enough. It feels like all my hard work is pointless if I don't meet these high standards. I know it’s irrational, but I can’t shake the fear that falling short means I’ll never succeed in the future. 

When you suggest exploring my interpretations, it makes sense in theory, but it’s hard to see how that will actually help me feel better. It’s not like reframing things will change the fact that I didn’t meet my own expectations.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a lot of fear tied to not meeting these high standards, as if your worth and future success depend entirely on perfection. While reframing won’t change the grade itself, it might help reduce the intensity of these distressing thoughts and the pressure you’re putting on yourself. Can you think of a time when something didn’t go perfectly, but things still turned out okay in the end?

client:
I guess there was that time I got a B on a history paper last semester. I was devastated at first, but I still passed the class. But that feels different because it wasn't as important as this upcoming exam - if I don't get an A this time, it could ruin my chances at grad school. 

The pressure feels so much higher now, and I don't know how to convince myself that "just okay" would be acceptable. Even thinking about settling for less than perfect makes me feel like I'm already failing.
therapist: It sounds like the stakes feel much higher this time, and the fear of not meeting your goal feels overwhelming. It might be helpful to explore whether this belief—that anything less than perfect could ruin your chances—is based on facts or assumptions. What evidence do you have that one exam grade alone would determine your future?

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's hard not to feel like this exam really will make or break my future. All the top grad programs look at GPA so closely, and I've heard horror stories about people missing their dream school by 0.1 points. The pressure makes my chest feel tight just thinking about it. 

I know logically one test shouldn't define me, but when I imagine getting even a B+, I can already feel the shame and panic rising. It's like my brain won't let me consider any other outcome besides perfection.
therapist: It sounds like this exam feels like a pivotal moment for you, and the fear of not meeting your goal is creating a lot of physical and emotional distress. While it’s true that GPA is a factor in grad school admissions, it’s rarely the only one—what other strengths or achievements do you think you bring to the table that might balance out this exam?

client: I know logically that grad schools look at more than just grades, but it's hard to believe that when I'm in the middle of this stress. I keep thinking about how everyone else in my program seems so much more put together, and I can't even imagine what I'd say in an application that would make up for a bad grade in this core class. The physical symptoms are the worst part - I actually threw up from nerves this morning before class.
therapist: It sounds like the comparison to others and the physical toll of this anxiety are making it even harder to see your own strengths clearly. When you think about what you’d write in an application, what’s something you’re proud of that has nothing to do with grades?

client: I guess I'm proud of how I've kept volunteering at the animal shelter even when I'm stressed about school. But it's hard to feel like that matters when everyone else seems to have these impressive internships and research projects. I worry that my application will just look weak in comparison.
therapist: It sounds like you're dismissing your own meaningful contributions—like your commitment to volunteering—because they don’t fit a narrow idea of what "counts" as impressive. That comparison trap can make it hard to recognize the unique qualities you bring. What do you think an admissions committee might appreciate about someone who sticks with their values, even under pressure?

client:
I guess I never really thought about it that way. But even if I stick to my values, doesn't that just make me naive? Everyone else seems to be playing the game and getting ahead while I'm stuck doing what feels right but gets me nowhere. 

It's hard to believe admissions committees would care about my volunteering when other applicants have research papers and internships at big companies. I feel like I'm falling behind by trying to do the "right" thing.
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught between honoring what feels meaningful to you and fearing that it won't "measure up" in a competitive system. But authenticity and consistency—like your dedication to the shelter—often reveal qualities like resilience and compassion that can’t be faked. What would it feel like to trust that those things matter just as much as the metrics you’re comparing yourself to?

client:
I know logically that compassion matters, but it's hard to really believe that when I see others getting ahead just by playing the game. Like at work, my coworker got promoted over me even though I know I put in more heart. It makes me wonder if being genuine actually holds me back. 

I want to trust that my values matter, but the system keeps rewarding the opposite—so how do I hold onto that belief when the evidence feels stacked against me? It makes me feel naive for caring about authenticity in the first place.
therapist: It sounds like your experiences—like the promotion at work—are making it hard to trust that authenticity and compassion are truly valued. It’s understandable to feel disheartened when the system seems to reward something different. What would it look like to balance staying true to your values while also advocating for yourself in ways that align with them?

client: Honestly, the idea of balancing my values with self-advocacy just makes me feel exhausted. Every time I try to "play the game" at work, it feels like I'm betraying myself—but when I don't, I get passed over. I don't even know what "aligned" self-advocacy would look like when the whole system feels rigged.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught in a painful either/or: feeling like you have to choose between betraying yourself or being overlooked. That exhaustion makes complete sense when the system feels so at odds with your values. What would it feel like to explore small ways of advocating for yourself that don't require compromising what matters most to you?

client:
I get what you're saying about small steps, but honestly it just feels like putting a bandaid on a much bigger issue. Every time I try to speak up even a little at work, I either get ignored or people act like I'm being difficult. It makes me feel like maybe I'm the problem after all. 

The idea of advocating for myself sounds exhausting when I don't even believe it'll make a difference. Like why bother if the system is just going to steamroll me anyway?
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling defeated and questioning whether your efforts matter, especially when it feels like the system dismisses or minimizes your voice. That sense of being "the problem" can be so isolating, but it’s worth exploring whether that belief is based on facts or the weight of these experiences. What would it feel like to focus first on reclaiming your sense of worth, separate from whether the system changes?
